title: Subscribe to Tabletop Battles Today!
content:
Something we don't do enough of here, we're told by adoring fans and business experts on digital engagement alike, is talk about what we do and how great we do it. Tabletop Battles is your favorite worker-owned media collective covering news and gaming in the wargaming, boardgaming, and increasingly the videogaming space, but we also do a lot more. We have an app! Let's talk about the app.

The Tabletop Battles App

If you haven't downloaded the app yet, you can get it for free through one of the links below:

We've been running this app and its associated cluster of services for six years now, and it's in the best place it's ever been, with support for the current editions of Warhammer 40K, Warhammer 40K Kill Team, Warhammer Age of Sigmar, Warhammer Horus Heresy, Warhammer The Old World, and non-Games Workshop titles Conquest: The Last Argument of Kings and the StarCraft Tabletop Miniatures Game. There are a number of apps out there for this kind of thing, though; why use ours?

  • Runs faster and better. Tabletop Battles is built in Flutter and not React. Flutter is less common but removes a lot of runtime jank that can bog down React Native apps. If you've noticed that TTBA runs faster, this is a primary reason why. Flutter generally outperforms React Native and uses less CPU and as a result, less battery.
  • Built-in stats screens. If you want more than just a list of your games, we've got you covered, and we're working on more personal stats you can access via our Edge web app.
  • Faction trackers. If you want to track things like Pain tokens or Saga progress, our app has that.
  • Other game modes. Do you want to play asymmetric missions? Track custom games? Do you need a different disposition than the one you're allowed to select? The Tabletop Battles interface is much more flexible, and allows for custom score input.
  • Direct feedback. We read every bug report and work to implement changes, and we respond to inquiries on Discord. The Tabletop Battles app is very much what you help make it.

It's the best app on the market for logging your games, useful both at the table and as a historical record keeper, letting you track your game state during play and check how things went after the fact.

But whatever. That's what the plebs get. If you subscribe to the Tabletop Battles Patreon at the $5 level, you get access to Administratum, our narrative play engine. Administratum turns the Tabletop Battles App into your one stop solution for roster management, campaign tracking, and progression recording across any kind of ongoing  tournament or narrative event. It used to be that Administratum was only designed to work with the Crusade 40K narrative play mode, but much like Crusade, that's a thing of the past -- with Administratum 4.0, you can use all of its tools to run Age of Sigmar, Trench Crusade, StarCraft, Necromunda, or anything else. Administratum 4.0 is currently live in an opt-in beta branch, and we'll be rolling out more of it in the coming months.

There are, however, levels to this game. And at the $10 Warhound Patron level, you get expanded access to Administratum with more roster slots, more modes to run your games in, and the ability to extend $5 tier Administratrum privileges to players in your campaign who aren't signed up at that level for the duration. There are a number of reasons we actually have more subscribers at the $10 tier than at the $5 tier, and this is just one of them: This is the level where you basically get everything we have to offer. If you go higher on your pledge however -- we do have $25 and $50 tiers for those of you with discernment and taste -- you get correspondingly larger allocations of Administratum resources. If you are a maniac who has decided to run a narrative campaign for literally 300 people, the Goku S-Class Gold ULTRA tier is right for you.

Subscriber-Only Content

Let's talk about what else being a $10 Warhound Patron gets you. Three times a week, we go behind the paywall to get deep and functional about playing competitive tabletop Warhammer 40K. Sometimes this involves talking about army lists that are big in the meta right now. Sometimes we dive deeper on a new Codex release with theorycrafting and test game results, or react to how a new Codex is affecting competitive events before the next Dataslate. A favorite topic for our army-specific writers is talking about how they play into certain opponents, or how they handle teams play with their army and their list's disposition choice. Here's an example, written by Innes Wilson back in August, that talks about playing the Take and Hold disposition with Space Marines, complete with a pair of example army lists and how they work; I've pulled it out from behind the paywall.

Our subscriber-only articles are written by competitive players who have success on the table; Ben Jurek, Orks afficionado, Top 10 ITC finisher the last three years, member of Team USA and recent winner of the Utah Cup writes for us, as does Isaac Terada, Las Vegas Teams Tournament finalist, podium finisher for the Challenger's Cup and second place behind Ben at that Utah Cup. Two co-founders of Stat Check, teams specialist Jeremy Curie (Champion's Cup, Toronto Team Open and BFS team wins in 2025, many other podiums, judging experience) and the aforementioned Innes (Top 10 ITC the last six years, Rank 1 ELO, Rank 1 ITC, 6 UKTC super major wins, way too many event wins to succinctly name here) write subscriber-only pieces for us. And when it comes time to be competitive on the hobby side of the table, Rob "TheChirurgeon" Jones has a cabinet full of Best Painted wins in addition to taking World Championship qualifier tickets in 2025 and 2026 and winning the Ettin Tabledtalk GT in 2025. Seriously, there's an actual cabinet.

Podcasts, Streaming, Video, No Ads

There are some things that are available to all our paid members, even those down on the $3 Every Bit Counts tier. First and foremost: No ads on the website. You go to the site, login through Patreon, and boom, they're gone, mobile and desktop. In addition, you get access to all our backer-exclusive podcasts, featuring the flagship offering HAMS Radio, where Rob and Norman talk about tabletop gaming (a lot of Trench Crusade recently, because Norman's our site lead on Trench Crusade), The Campaign Trail podcast which covers narrative campaign gaming, and anything else we decide to record a short series on. As a backer you can also hop into our livestreams whenever we're video gaming, like when Rob and Norman played through all of Boltgun 2 on stream recently.

That's the Pitch

We do cool shit here! We want to keep doing cool shit, more and better! Worker-owned and worker-operated bottom-up businesses like ours live and die on our valued leaders, because we don't have corporate overlords to bail us out if, oh, someone goes and destroys the entire digital advertising industry because they wanted to put a demon chatbot into their search engine. Hypothetically speaking. If you think we're cool and you get value out of what we do, and any of the above sounds like it would also be cool to have in your back pocket (or front pocket, or purse, or wherever you keep your phone, which is where the Internet lives), we'd love to have you onboard.

We'll be doing more posts like these in the future, but they won't be all the same; we've got some more ideas cooking up in the oven to make your support mean even more. Til then.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: [Review] Silver Pines: Does the Exquisite Corpse Dream?
content:
Stop me if you've heard this one before: Lone detective is dispatched to a small town along the edge of the Pacific Northwest to locate the supposed last witness of a missing girl beloved by the community. Wait, shit, did I mention he doesn't remember how exactly he got into town, that the town itself is dense with nightmarish and inhuman denizens, that any other actual human contact is rare, and the detective's conversations with them are simultaneously dense and airy in the sort of way that only a conversation half remembered from a dream upon waking is? All to get him too embroiled within a tangled snarl of too many mysteries to solve, but which each contain a kernel of what feels like a clue towards the true fate of that missing girl.

Some of you are now thinking about Twin Peaks, others Alan Wake, and perhaps a few of Silent Hill. As with many entries within the survival horror genre, these reference points are a deliberate attempt to establish a trusted shorthand with you, the player. Unlike many of those contemporaries however, Silver Pines is not a game interested in using this shorthand to establish anything other than familiarity. There is no lore to establish, no wiki to inform. Silver Pines, at its best, is a game where the point is in the playing.

All just things. Just a dressing room, just a mirror, just a lockbox, just a phone, just a man.

Gameplay

Much as its introductory elements do, the gameplay of Silver Pines should feel familiar on multiple levels. The map you traverse evokes Metroidvania gameplay, with nonlinear exploration and multiple early impassable landmarks of note to remind you that yes, you’d be wise to return later when you have the right tool. Though even now it feels awkward to ascribe any of the gameplay elements to any one gameplay style or genre convention, as so many of this game’s forebears have worked to blend and blur the already softly permeable lines of genre together. Is Resident Evil 2 a Metroidvania? Is Signalis? Not according to the tags on Steam, and yet both share consistent similarities in both gameplay and traversal with this game, which does have that tag applied.

You have an ever-expanding but still deliberately stifling inventory system, where items take up a number of squares. You have melee weapons that double as utility items, that break down through use. There’s persistence to the enemies found upon the map, and some particularly aggressive subtypes can follow you from room to room, zone to zone, if not dealt with. The items that provide passive bonuses to your abilities (traversal, combat, and so on) are all tied to the protagonist’s sense of self. Variations on variations, again and again. Everything is familiar, and yet it's all done so well that I can’t find myself complaining about it.

Your ever-expanding inventory, and its ever diminishing free space.

A mechanic for which I found myself increasingly thankful was the ability for Red Walker to take polaroid pictures of areas or items of note withing the environment, thereby adding them to your map. This is great to reference later as you find the tools to address specific obstacles, or just to piece together specific puzzles without needing to consistently backtrack through a dangerous environment.

Silver Pines also features one of my favorite combat mechanics to date (itself evoking Alone in the Dark), wherein each bullet must be manually reloaded with timed button clicks, and each damaged weapon must be duct-taped back together in much the same way. Yes, it’s fully possible to avoid these mechanics by doing all your reloading in the inventory screen at a safehouse security box, but sooner or later your character will need to reload in a tense situation. You’ll need to make space for yourself, just so you can get Red Walker to chug a soda or slam another slug into his shotgun. You’ll misjudge, take damage, and then resort to a desperate flurry of dodging around enemy attacks and striking with melee. Then your melee weapon breaks. This friction might not be for everyone, but I found myself enjoying the struggle and, again, the experience.

Who is she? Where is she?

Visuals

The game has a deeply interesting art style, utilizing soft cell-shaded avatars for gameplay and blurred watercolors for the cutscenes or character portraits. I wasn’t initially certain how I felt about this fusion, but as the game went on I found it draw me in more and more. Whether it was the many-layered environments, where later areas can be constantly seen in the landscape as you traverse, or the use of coherency within the watercolor to communicate a character’s emotional state or possible drifting humanity.

Thanks.

Cast

I really can’t go on without including praise for the voice acting team, whose skills really sing through the entire narrative. Suzi Hunter in particular is a standout here in her portrayal of a figure whose enigmatic nature seems to sit outside the constant loop of hostility and judgement of all other characters whom Red Walker interacts with throughout the story. Speaking of Red, Chase Brown puts a truly transformative twist into his delivery here, allowing the character of Red to slowly warm up to the world around him alongside the player with an alarmingly engaging performance.

James. Dale. Alan. Johnny. Red.

Horror

In Silver Pines, the enemies are shadow creatures, whose lack of fully distinct features set them apart at once from the world around them. Some appear human, others decidedly less so, and while their physicality is beautifully animated, their true aura of dread comes from each of their unique audio cues. Whether keening moans, aggressive and feral growls, or distorted screeches whose voices overwhelm all other ambient sound, I found them all extremely well-crafted for both the mood and narrative.

As with most horror games, there’s obviously a point you’ll reach where these enemies lose their intimidation factor, and risk stepping into either the area of frustration or predictable obstacle. For what its worth however, I personally found that once I found my rhythm, each enemy became a new puzzle piece in the mystery of Silver Pines, even if they lost their horror edge by the end.

Just things. Just a lockbox, just a man, just a ferry, just a town. All blurred by a storm everyone else saw coming.

Audio

As I’ve mentioned throughout this article thus far, I have nothing but praise for the audio of Silver Pines. Whether the soundtrack, whose ambient tracks work excellently to maintain tone, the shocking and sometimes deafening reports of gunfire, or the satisfying squelch of Red Walker’s boot crushing a monster’s head into the cement. It all works.

Special praise, however, is due for a particular song that appears early in the game, and whose haunting presence remains a looming shadow across the remainder. I won’t spoil it here, but I found that it captured the energy of those affecting tracks found in the works of David Lynch, or many of the works inspired by his own.

Emotional Truth Over Logical Reason

Much ink has been put to paper in regards to the nature of videogames as an artform, and whilst I think that the medium is irrefutably art, there’s something to be said for its typical adherence to logic or what we would refer to as the real. It makes sense, as most games are by themselves an abstraction of a simulation. You might have never held a gun before, but if you’ve played an fps or five, you likely have an expectation for the realities of the function of a firearm. Some developers afford time to focus on the detail or accuracy of reloading, to better thin the abstraction and heighten the simulation to this end. Fewer games, in my experience, are interested in the emotional truth behind the gun.

This makes sense, as this truth can be hard to convey in a universal (or perhaps marketable) way. Someone might find power in the same moment another find fear and anxiety. Both are the truth, but neither is the same, but both are the same. Dreams and emotions both blur their edges when it comes to truth, and we as human beings deserve art that grasps at those edges, or at least guides our hands to blend them. Silver Pines, by the end of my playthrough, felt like that.

An Experience Worth Having

We come to the end of our review, and if any of this writing or the game it described appealed to you or even piqued a fleeting interest, I encourage you to give the game a chance. If you do that last bit, and decide to experience Silver Pines, I invite you to experience all of it. If I’ve earned your trust as critic or a writer, or the game feels as though it has done the same, please look up as little more as you can, play of much of it as there is, and try to find all three endings. There’s truth in them, I feel, when seen altogether.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Horus Heresy Legions Astartes Primary Detachments
content:
Behold, Games Workshop has delivered unto the Legions Astartes a PDF containing new Primary Detachments. You can download it right now on the Warhammer Community site and I recommend you do. There are also new Core Missions for all Heresy players to use, which we will cover separately.

As you have access to the rules for free we can discuss them in full here. You can go ahead and use them straight away… or at least as soon as you can bring the required models to a table.

We also have a new Core Mission Pack and we’ll be looking at that separately. That affects all factions whereas these Detachments are only for the Legions.

We get five new Primary Detachments, all based heavily on what used to be called Rites of War in previous editions. The new Detachments are:

  • Pride of the Legion - Loads of Veterans and Terminators. 
  • Fury of the Ancients - Dreadnoughts.
  • Sky-hunter Phalanx - Jetbikes, speeders and planes. 
  • Armoured Spearhead - Tanks.
  • Orbital Drop Assault - Drop pods, with a caveat that you should agree ahead of the game before using it.

How to Use the New Detachments

You build your whole army around your Primary Detachment. One of these new ones would entirely replace your usual Crusade Primary Detachment. You’ll have a new Detachment with some troops and a variety of other stuff but you don’t get those usual Troop and transport slots that you’re used to and you may not be able to get them at all. All let you bring a High Command and two Command choices, one of which is Prime, except the Armoured Spearhead. That has three Command slots but no Prime slots of any kind.

Each of these new Primary Detachments severely limits the type of Additional Detachments you can take. They each tend to list a few things that are allowed but that leaves out an awful lot of stuff. Expect to find maybe one Apex and a few Auxiliary Detachments on the list for each.

None of these new Primary Detachments allow Allied Detachments, the Detachments that you get from your Legion’s Rite of War or the ones that characters like the Champion or Esoterist can unlock. They also don’t allow any Prime Advantage to add units to a Detachment in your army, meaning you can’t take Logistical Benefits or the extra units that people like Alpha Legion or Shattered Legions can unlock. No Assassins, either.

So now that we’ve got that out of the way, let’s look at what fun new things these Detachments do now allow.

Pride of the Legion

You get three Retinue, five Heavy Assault and five Elites slots. One of each of the Heavy Assault and Elites slots is Prime, which is great as Prime Heavy Assault slots are pretty rare. Additionally, Any unit with Vanguard (X) can swap it out for Line (1) during army selection. If a Traitor army wants to deploy a massive unit of True Believers Cataphractii with Line they now can.

Word Bearers Cataphractii Terminator Squad - Credit: RichyP

You also get to take a Heavy Transport for every Retinue, Heavy Assault or Elites unit you bring. However you can’t take any other Detachments other than Officer Cadre, Shock Assault, Heavy Support, Warlord or a Lord of War that has to have a transport capacity - which rules out most of them. You won’t be able to bring any tanks, planes (Except maybe a Caestus) or even Rhinos. You might also miss characters like Apothecaries and Techmarines, though you could potentially bring Commanders like a Master of the Forge to fix your Land Raiders.

The good news is that you probably don’t need any fancy stuff. There are a ton of options between Retinues, Heavy Assault and Elites, covering a lot of possibilities. Land Raiders and Spartans can also do a lot of work. You may well be able to get a 3,000 point army without any extra Detachments so you can save on any character taxes.

The army has to bring a Master of the Legion. It’s a little bit annoying to have to bring a Praetor, as you almost certainly don’t need to unlock an Officer Cadre, which is the only Apex Detachment you’re allowed. You could just have an Auxiliary Detachment with your Praetor. You could also have a Primarch as your Warlord and bring no other characters at all if you wanted.

Finally, your opponent gets a VP for every Elites or Heavy Assault unit they destroy. Not for Retinues, for some reason. This is another reason to have all your people tucked up safely inside Land Raiders.

The main strength of this list is probably the access to Line on Terminators and maybe things like Veteran Breachers. Line is a bit less essential in the new mission pack but this army can do any of the new missions perfectly well.

Fury of the Ancients

This gives you slots for your characters, a Retinue and ten Dreadnoughts, two of which can be Prime. There’s a new Prime Advantage Ancient of War, giving a Dreadnought Eternal Warrior (1), which is excellent.

Salamanders Dreadnoughts Credit: McWhat

Again you aren’t allowed much else. You can only have Command and Specialist units if they’re Battlesmiths. Your only other Detachment options are Techmarine Covenants, War Engines and a Lord of War with a transport capacity. You can add extra units with Prime Advantages, but only War-engines. And again, every Dreadnought that dies gives your opponent a VP.

You need a character to be your Warlord so you can’t only take Dreadnoughts. It probably makes sense to bring a Retinue so they have somewhere safe-ish to be, though the unit can’t have a transport other than a Lord of War. A Deep-striking Saturnine Retinue might be a way to keep your Warlord alive. They’ll attract basically every small arms weapon your opponent has, as they’re basically useless against Dreadnoughts. so they’d better be tough..

I know the community wanted this Detachment and it’s thematically very cool. But for actual gameplay I think it could be a problem. Someone can put down ten or twelve Dreadnoughts and not much else, which leaves a lot of units on the opposite side with no real way of participating in the game. It’s not fun to fire at something needing a 6 to wound and hoping the target then rolls a 1 for its save.

Sky-hunter Phalanx

You get the usual characters, two Retinues and ten Fast Attack slots, two of which are Prime, gaining access to a new Skilled Riders Prime Advantage, which gives them Shrouded (6+). I think it’s a slight shame this isn’t available for the retinue slots, as you’d think those guys would be good on their jetbikes.

White Scars Golden Keshig. Credit - Soggy

The restrictions here are especially heavy. You can only add First Strike, Combat Pioneer or Lord of War choices. Every unit has to either have the Antigrav sub-type, be a Flyer itself or begin the game in a flyer. There isn’t much you can do with the Recon slots from the Combat Pioneer Detachment, beyond sticking some recon guys in a storm eagle, I suppose. Your retinues can be the legacy guys on jetbikes, use jump packs or arrive in a plane.

White Scars get a couple more options. They can swap Retinue slots for Elites and take Golden Keshig units or swap Fast Attack Slots for Support Slots to get Kyzagan Assault Speeders.

I think this will create armies that are basically fine. I don’t think this lets you spam anything all that problematic other than the retinues, which are nasty but which any other army has access to anyway. Jetbikes and speeders are perfectly ok but every army will have some tools to deal with them. Spamming a lot of flyers could be nasty but eventually they’ll run out of fuel/ammo and stop turning up.

The army kind of relies on using the new mission pack. In the core rules Cavalry can’t score objectives, which would be awkward for an all-cavalry army. That restriction is now gone, which is very nice for jetbikes and speeders. You’ll need to be a bit careful about the enemy scoring Vanguard too easily if you put something like 3 bikes or a speeder on an objective though.

Armoured Spearhead

This really is an army of tanks and almost nothing else. You get a High Command and three Command slots, a Support slot and ten Armour slots. There are no Prime slots. You can add Armoured Support, Combat Pioneer, First Strike, Techmarine Covenant, Armoured Fist and Lord of War Detachments. However, you can only have units that are either Vehicles or have Battlesmith (X), meaning you are limited to having a few Techmarines here and there, who won’t have any units to join.

White Scars Fellblade and friends. Credit - Soggy

So what do you do with your High Command and Character slots? Well you stick Decurions in them. Tanks with Decurions can fill Command slots and you can have a unit with a Decurion Magna fill the High Command slot. I don’t think this actually changes those units’ battlefield roles, however, so a Lord of War with a Decurion Magna filling a High Command slot would still count against your 25% maximum to spend on Lords of War.

The final special rule is Squadron Tactics. Vehicles within 6” of other vehicles get +2 to their repair rolls. That’s really handy, obviously. You may not need to take many Techmarines to fix your tanks thanks to this, though it would probably be useful to have at least a couple here and there.

I think this detachment could be a bit of a problem if people decide to max out AV14. There’s nothing to stop you taking an army of nine or ten Kratos here, which would be rubbish to play against. The previous version had to be based more around Predator and/or Sicarans, which was a bit more interactive. I hope that people don’t treat this Detachment as a license to misbehave at their opponents’ cost.

Some of the issues here are with the rules for Vehicles themselves. In particular, the fact that smaller tanks like Predators want to sit still to maximise the power of their Heavy guns but big ones like the Kratos can cruise around and fire at full effect. You wouldn’t want to create a game in which tanks just sat still and shot at each other. Unfortunately that tends to push the Armoured Company player to field more Kratos and Super-heavies, though they are some of the least interactive units for opponents to play against.

Orbital Drop Assault

The Drop Pod Detachment is really odd and the rules don’t quite work unless I’m misunderstanding them, which is certainly possible. The PDF tells us that these are essentially a beta version of rules that will be published later at some point. I hope to see significant revision when that happens to fix some mechanical and balance issues as much as possible.

Credit: JD Reynolds

The Detachment is very varied. You get your usual characters, a Retinue, two each of Troops, Elites and Heavy Assault, one each of which is Prime, plus two Support slots. Every non-vehicle unit you take lets you bring a Transport or Heavy Transport.

There aren’t any restrictions on what you can put in all these slots. However, every unit with Deep Strike or Orbital Assault Vehicle has to start the game in Reserves and flyers have to start in Aerial Reserves. Everything else has to be inside a transport in either type of Reserves or else it’s immediately destroyed at the start of the game. So are any empty pods.

Essentially the deal is that all (or most of, see the table) your Drop Pods come down during Deployment rather than during the game. The Drop Pods’ opponent gets to deploy first and then you Deep Strike all your pods. You first drop in any Deathstorm Pods, shoot their guns and then bring in your other pods. Your other reserves arrive from turn 2 onwards, though any number of units can Deep Strike on any given turn, not just one per turn.

Whenever you Deep Strike a unit you roll on the Orbital Drop Table, which determines whether your unit arrives at all and how much it scatters. You get +1 to these rolls during Deployment, which is good as a roll of a 1 means the unit doesn’t arrive and no others can either. A roll of a 2 still means the unit doesn’t arrive and will have to come in from turn 2 onwards when normal reserves rolls happen.

The rules for the Impact Reactive Doors on Drop Pods say that passengers have to get out during the following move sub-phase. But the Orbital Drop Assault player is going second, meaning that during their opponent’s first turn their army hasn’t had a move sub-phase yet and everyone is still inside the pods. I don’t know if it’s intended that everyone stays in their pods through the first enemy turn, but that seems to be the case for now.

I think that by current RAW you can make disordered charges from the pods in your turn 1. All the restrictions on charging after Deep Strike talk about rules for during the turn in which the pod came down. The pod didn’t come down in a turn at all so that can’t apply. They’d be disordered charges though, due to disembarking.

It’s rough that the other army gets the first turn. You’ll probably have a lot of slow-ish foot infantry scattered around the place and your opponent will have a combined force that may be able to outmanoeuvre you. There’s a serious risk of having all your recently-deployed infantry killed as they clamber out of burning pods. Your best option is probably setting up close-ish to the enemy in positions from which you can take objectives and advance, rather than right in front of the enemy guns. Traitor players may wish to avoid dropping in too close to Custodes and everyone should be aware of the threats they’re deploying close to.

You can keep back some jump pack units if you want and try to do a mass deep strike on Turn 2. But the more of these units you bring the less you'll be dropping at the start and the weaker you'll be in those early turns. Deep Strike is still not great for Assault units as they can't charge when they arrive, so they'll never be in melee before turn 3 - after your opponent has had three full turns already.

I don’t know if the designers have thought through all the implications of all this. Deploying pods in the deployment phase is fine in theory but it causes a bunch of problems. For example, you can’t intercept pods that come down during deployment, because it isn’t your opponent’s turn so you’re not the Reactive player and can’t do Reactions. That might not matter though, as they'll do huge damage to your army as it sits helplessly inside drop pods.

So for now this is a slight mess that needs a bit more thought and clarification. That’s fine for what are essentially playtesting rules. Personally I wouldn’t go out and buy a load of drop pods thanks to this by the way, as these rules are going to be reviewed, hopefully soon. If you have a bunch of pods in a cupboard then by all means give this a go, then send GW your feedback on the game.

Final Thoughts

These new FOCs do a good job of bringing back the lists you could make with the old Rites of War. If anything, they’re more restrictive than those used to be and allow for even more skew. There are good and bad outcomes from all this.

Thousand Sons Legion Saturnine Dreadnought - credit: Colin Ward

Starting with the good, you can make very thematic lists now. New ways of building armies will breathe life into the game and give all of us different ways to play. I’m keen to see what I can make as a Pride of the Legion list for my Imperial Fists for example, perhaps featuring Dorn and Sigismund.

The problem is that skew lists don’t tend to result in good games. The majority of these lists are virtually immune to small arms fire from units like tactical squads. They aren’t necessarily more powerful than an army made using the Crusade Primary Detachment but they introduce an element of rock/paper/scissors to games that not everyone enjoys. Personally I like a game where I don’t know who’s won till quite late on and I’m not sure these lists provide that.

Much of this really comes down to players. If you choose to field a wall of AV14 or Plasma Contemptors you can’t expect to get many games, as people won’t like playing against you. Unfortunately this places the responsibility for deciding what’s fair on us as players rather than on GW, to whom we pay loads of money to write rules.

It’s interesting that they’ve given us these unfinished rules for Drop Pod armies. It’s an interesting insight into the design process I suppose. It’s also a good example of how the Heresy team can write an awful lot of words without quite managing to explain a set of rules. To be honest I’m not sure a drop assault can ever be a balanced rule for standard missions. I don’t think past versions were much fun either. We’ll see where they end up with this.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Adeptus Mechanicus Legends Datasheets
content:
The Legends roster for the Adeptus Mechanicus is fairly slim, made up of units drawn from a defunct Forgeworld resin upgrade kit, the hangers-on to the old Techmarine kit, and even our beloved delivery drill. When these were legal, you'd really only see them as complements to existing alpha strike gameplans, or backfield bodies made to deny Deep Strikes; not a ton was lost in the shift of these units to Legends, with the caveat that it further reduced the strength of Cult Mechanicus-themed Admech forces compared to the rank & file of the Skitarii.

Many players still treasure their Terrax, and more still have used units like X-101 as part of conversions, so today we're stepping into the narrative side of 40k and examining what the factions gains with added access to these Legends of the Adeptus Mechanicus.

Characters

X-101

Admech X-101. Credit: Pendulin

Starting off strong, we have X-101 from the Blackstone Fortress expansion, Escalation. X-101 was the first real look we got at what would become the modern aesthetic for Servitors, further expanded upon with the fantastic Servitor Battleclade unit most Lords of the Forge lists run 2-3 of. He essentially acts as a Support, being attached to a unit containing a Tech-Priest Infantry model during the Formation step, but can be attached in addition to a Leader+Support. Why does that matter? Well, packing what amounts to a BS 2+ mini-version of the Kataphron Destroyer's heavy Grav-cannon isn't the worst thing to add to a unit led by a Manipulus, but the real sell is in melee: X-101 swings with a modest 2 attacks, but usually at 3+/S8/-2/3. With the Cult Mechanicus keyword, we can slot him into Data-Psalm Conclave, and provide his squad an extra +1A/+1S on the charge, which really starts to look appetizing alongside a kitted-out squad of Fulgurite Electro-Priests.

Both of the Legends Servitor units have Mindlock, which affords them an extra +1WS/+1BS while in a unit led by a Tech-Priest. For normal Servitors, which we'll cover shortly, this brings them up to par with other profiles (and even then, not really), but X-101 is special in that he starts at BS 3+/WS 4+, meaning that coupled with the Conqueror Doctrina, he's able to hit on 2s in both shooting and melee when alongside a Tech-Priest, making up for the relatively low number of attacks. For 40pts in Lords of the Forge or Data-Psalm Conclave, he's a solid enough rate if your aim is to build a deathstar unit, chucking him with a pricey priest as ablative wounds which hit on 2s.

Infantry

Servitors

Servitors saw play in essentially every army that could utilize them, being at any given time one of the cheapest pieces to set and forget in an important section of the board. In this sense, they embodied the Imperium's philosophy perfectly, being more useful as pieces of meat at the right place, than possessing intrinsic value. These are taken as a single 4-model set, and are attached like X-101 to a Tech-Priest Enginseer-led unit during the declare Formations step (but only one Servitor bodyguard per Enginseer). This faces a couple of issues, which start with the fact that Enginseers tend not to lead units—you lose out on Lone Operative, which tends to keep them alive better than their attached unit's bulk. Moreover, Enginseers don't really benefits the squad they're leading, meaning that you can't float things like the Dominus' 5+++ onto these otherwise frail extra wounds.

Techpriest Enginseer and Servitors. Credit: SRM

It's not all bad, though, because the weaponry mounted to this unimpressive package is genuinely quite good. Half of the squad can swap their Servo-arms for your choice of Multi-melta, Heavy Bolter, or Plasma Cannon. The star here is the Multi-meltas, which Admech can send up the board via our Dunerider in a package of Enginseer+Electro-Priests+Servitors. You're still only hitting on 4s at best, but with the wound rerolls you're almost always going to convert successful shots into huge damage. Ultimately I think this falls short outside of exactly Data-Psalm Conclave (which really just wants more reasonable Cultmech melee), but that's largely because you can only associate Servitors with Enginseers. At their price of 50pts/4, if they could stand alone, or alongside other Tech-Priests, we'd really be talking.

Secutarii Hoplites

Ah, the titan-guard. Hoplites were made to stride forth alongside the largest of Imperial Knights, and serve as a solid wall of chaff for your Adeptus Titanicus units. With something big potentially coming to plastic in the future, it's worth noting that Secutarii still exist in the lore. In any case, for 65/130 you get 5-10 Vanguard-equivalent profiles with two major changes, being their 4++ save, and access to [Anti-Vehicle 4+, Devastating Wounds] in both shooting and melee. While it's still just 1 damage, and only 1-2 attacks depending on the profile, this is a frightening thing to be able to take en masse, and allows you to chip through Vehicles while relying on a 4++ squad to hold the line. Add in a Dominus, and suddenly you're looking at a shockingly beefy unit, not unlike Dominus-led Fulgurites. The trade-off is that your Hoplites' spears are lower in Strength and Damage, but in return pack Anti-Vehicle and the Skitarii keyword.

The reason these look better than the mediocre Fulgurites, however, stems from their ability: Titan-Guard. You get a free Heroic Intervention with this squad, for any number of Hoplites in a given turn, even re-rolling the charge if you have a Titan. In this way, you can use them in 5-model squads as a punishing piece for opponents looking to alpha strike you, potentially tying up or otherwise cracking back against early threats. These are still worse than, say, either flavor of Sicarian for the role, but their 4++ can make math awkward into elite armies.

Secutarii Peltasts

The Peltasts are a lot more appetizing than their Hoplite kin, coming in at 50/100 for 5-10, and one of the army's worst save profiles, with a meager T3/5+/6++. They wield Galvanic Casters, which either fire 5 S4 shots with [Assault], or 2 S5 shots with [Heavy] and -1 AP. In either case, these suffer from being Damage 1, but I'd be lying if I said the 5-shot mode wasn't nice to have. S4 is worse against MEQs now, but you do get to take an Omnispex (both Secutarii can) so you're usually hitting on 4s at worst. 50pts for 25 shots' worth of mulched Toughness 3 foes is nice, and as an added bonus, you can dole out -1 to hit to any one Infantry unit hit by your Galvanic Casters' shots. Again, we're talking about a 50pt unit with the Skitarii keyword, so these don't need to do much to see consideration purely on the merits of their pricetag.

In 11th Edition, negative hit modifiers are pretty nice to have, as getting Cover's -1BS can outright deny shooting phases from some of the game's scariest deathstars. They have gotten worse in the context of Marines' sweeping Toughness change, it's true, but for 50pts these would see serious play if fully legal, just as action monkeys which occasionally make a Sternguard brick rather sad. Admech's previous cheap action tool—Servitor Battleclade—has slowly crept up in points to the extent it's really more a tool for Lords of the Forge than for the faction at large. Having a Skitarii-keyworded equivalent that's 10pts cheaper than even the initial cost of Clade would be fantastic, and if you're playing with Legends legal, this is a serious consideration during listbuilding.

Vehicles

Terrax-Pattern Termites. Credit: Pendulin

Terrax-Pattern Termite

Finally, the assault drill. Coming in at a whopping 200pts, this glorified Drop Pod delivers up to 12 models' worth of non-Kataphron Adeptus Mechanicus Infantry up the board, historically being blobs of Vanguard. For those not around for its reign, the Terrax was an absolute menace in 9th Edition, and giving Admech the capacity to deliver otherwise-slow threats up the board is something the design team has been careful about since then. In any case, this is a T10, 14 Wound behemoth that usually packs a pair of Heavy Flamers and its signature Terrax Melta Cutter, which is effectively a 5-shot Multi-Melta equivalent to the kind wielded by our Servitors. Not only that, but it packs S14 in melee (if you can physically fit it there), so it poses a problem to big threats if you sink a charge after clearing screens with the flamers.

When this sheet was designed, Hastarii were but a twinkle in the designers' eyes, but looking at the Terrax with them in mind it's patently horrifying to see the sheer density of firepower we can deliver out of nowhere. Popping up with 2x5 Marshalled Fusileers and clearing a Knight & change is a very real concern, and even fishing for a 7-8 with Ruststalkers' innate charge bonus could make sense. Being far tougher than any other Admech Dedicated Transport, it also serves as one of the best targets for Explorator Maniple's Reactive Safeguard stratagem (and of course, Haloscreed's reactive move) in terms of Vehicles to re-embark. Ultimately, this is likely the unit missed most from the transition of the army's resin models to Legends, although given the faction's performance in 9th Edition it at least went out with a bang.

Final Thoughts

There's a bit of a cybernetic elephant in the room regarding Admech's Legends roster, and it's the fact that a decent chunk of the playerbase clamors for the addition of the Mechanicum's unique robots to the range in some capacity. I see where this comes from—you see a cool robot, and are told you cannot play with the cool robot—but in the grand scheme of 40k Admech is a fairly developed range at this point, and doesn't really need that shot in the arm.

As for the existing Legends sheets, nothing is outright broken when compared to current combos, and while I'd maybe caution against a player taking ~2x5 Peltasts as extremely efficient secondary play pieces, the role they play will rarely feel game-determinative. You shave 25pts off of a Battleclade and give it the Skitarii keyword, and get even better at what Admech already excel at: Doing actions. The Terrax is a ton of fun, albeit properly-costed at 200pts, and X-101 is a neat little way to add extra oompf to your Cult Mechanicus force. Really the only major miss is in the form of the Hoplites, and even so they're likely going to throw out at least a couple mortal wounds at a Vehicle before biting the bullet. Running them alongside a Dominus and maybe even a Marshal in Eradication Cohort would be totally passable, as far as narrative lists are concerned. Many of these sheets' issues stem from being associated with the worst codex of 10th Edition, and receiving very little in the way of updates since then.

Overall rating, C.

Archetype

Eliminator Ultrawatch

Thoughts

Our top four here is completed by Ultrawatch, albeit with a few shakeups from the norm. Florian's version cuts Calgar, removing the need for Terminator Storm Force, and instead builds a central brawler stack with Victrix/Cato/Caius, and augments the list's shooting with triple Eliminators and Shadow Force. With Guilliman's re-rolls, these are in fact a nightmare for their price tag, and provide a deep well of board presence to keep the build active even when the foe strikes back hard. Cool to see some experimentation with the formula, and well done to Florian.

Archetype

C'tanless Cursed

Thoughts

Necrons wave their blood-stained banners as one of the few non-Marine/Imperium factions that are really thriving right now, deploying a high threat Destroyer build to crush the competition. Double Lokhusts gives you reliable damage into everything, and here rather than a C'tan, they're rolling with a Wrath squad to tarpit foes, and some powerful Characters in support.  These choices free up some points for a Skorpekh unit, which is a really solid trade piece to have, and also for a big Ophydian unit, a surprisingly lethal Ingress threat when they're S6 that can flex to scoring as required. With the metagame so lethal at the moment Wraiths really are the only thing that can reliably tarpit in the Necron roster (even more so than C'tan), so I'm not surprised to see this doing well, and it's going onto the list of builds I might audible into if my testing of other WCW armies crashes out. Do I want to paint three more Ophydians? No. But I might. Congratulations Kalle.

Thoughts

Welp, they've not given me a complex one this week. These are two primarily melee builds that are going to slam into each other in a spectacular orgy of violence. One is going to win. The Orks have the upside of some guns that actually matter. The Wolves advantage is that their depth of viciousness is significantly higher and that saga of the Beastslayer is great here, turning those regular Wulfen into all-purpose blenders. The Wolves having 2x10 (really 4x5) Grey Hunters as their scoring pieces really helps too, as they can comically bully Grotz, and aren't half bad at depleting Boyz.

The foundational issue for the Orks here is that if the Marines keep 2CP up, answering that big terminator brick is just not really doable. Only the Killsaw Nobz or Ghaz can really make a dent, and the former are vulnerable to AoC, while the latter won't kill all of them. Both units will then suffer a tremendous counterattack. If the Orks play cagier, the obnoxious reach of the super biker Wulfen squad gives the Wolves agency to either gradually pick them off, or choose battles they can win. This ends up feeling like a pretty serious mismatch, especially as in the T&H mirror, the Orks cannot avoid having a fight, and the consequences were broadly as expected.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Whiskerwood
content:
NOTE: This game is currently in Early Access, and this review deals only with the state of the game as it exists in late 2026; when the game is released into 1.0, we may revisit this review.

I’ve previously talked about my abiding love of city-building games in my review of Timberborn, and I am an absolute hog when it comes to games about assembling an increasingly complicated metropolis. In a few ways, Whiskerwood and Timberborn have a lot in common - a citybuilder in a voxel environment with anthropomorphised animal pops, plus verticality and stacking buildings - but while Timberborn is set in the dawning of a post-humanity apocalypse, Whiskerwood takes place in a quasi-17th century world, and while the beavers of Timberborn appear to be entirely alone and isolated in their settlements, masters of all they survey, in Whiskerwood, your “Whiskers” (Mice) are decidedly not.

For you see, the Whiskers of Whiskerwood are colonists, yes, but they are subalterns (in the Gramscian sense) of a greater empire, and, as well as being town planner and resource manager, the player in their role as the chief of these Whiskers (the “Tail”, i.e, you) must function as a sort of intermediary between the oppressed Whiskers and their oppressors, the “Claws” (Cats) and (to a lesser degree) the Weasels. The Claws function as a distant aristocratic overclass, while the Weasels tend towards seafaring renegades, pirates, traders, and smugglers.

From such humble beginnings...

You begin your colony by choosing one of three different starting states. Far Frontier is what you’d call the “standard” game; the state dispatches fewer loyalists, but smugglers demand more goods. Then there's Pirate Seas, which has more pirate ransom requests but tax ships are more infrequent and smuggled goods fetch better prices. Finally, in Monarch Loyalists, the state dispatches far more Monarchist whiskers, and they are willing to tolerate more hardship in general, but are fundamentally anti-industry.

With a scenario selected and a map generated, you can choose a virgin island (the size of which can be altered at the game’s start), abundant in some resources and lacking in others, in a local archipelago and from there, building out your colony the way you’d expect, beginning with access to primitive houses and gathering structures, with a limited get-started packet of resources, so far so normal, this is the ground floor of every colony sim, but what’s this? Two days from now, the Claws will send their envoy for your first.. tax payment? Yes, the cats want taxes from you, and they’re charging you for the supplies you arrived on the island with, plus the costs for the colonists’ passage.

Where the focus of many other citybuilders and colony sims lies on accumulating resources to make your pops happy, to survive the winter, and level up your buildings, in Whiskerwood you’re required to do that while also satisfying the ever-increasing material demands of your feline overlords. Your tax requirement starts on day two and continues every two days, with the exception of Winter, when the cats can’t be bothered to sail to your island (but don’t worry, they’ll add up the tax they don’t take in that time and take it as a lump sum from the survivors when Spring comes, thank-you-very-much).

The way taxes are calculated in Whiskerwood is laid out by the developer, and depends on five variables:

  • Population (a flat rate of 3 coins per day per Whisker)
  • Administrative (13 coins to begin with, increasing by 0.3 for every day survived past the first)
  • Travel (21 coins per colonist ship that turns up)
  • Production (10% of the value of all industrial production)
  • Supply (cost of goods accepted from the supply ship - more on that later).

So, in the absence of some mass die-off event (which can happen; winter is a thing after all), the tax bill is pretty much always going to climb day by day, visit by visit, becoming an increasingly difficult burden to meet as your colony grows.

The logic of colonialism has a high body count

Since the developers of Whiskerwood understand that the primary purpose of a colony in the eye of the parent state is primary sector resource extraction, that is the cats’ sole interest in your case too; although you’ll need to refine resources and manufacture goods and services to keep your whiskers happy and healthy, the cats have absolutely no interest in that nonsense and will not accept any of them as part of a tax payment; in fact, what the cats will accept doesn’t really change throughout the game (with a minor exception), they want logs, they want coal and ores, they want cotton and flax, they want raw fish and berries. Later in the game, when the naval aspect begins to kick off, the cats will add a desire for canvas sails and bronze nails to their list of acceptable payments. Everything else? No, thank you!

This adds an interesting rub to resource management in Whiskerwood. Yes, you need planks for anything more than the most basic construction, and you’ll definitely use them - but if you turn all your logs into the more useful planks, how will you pay your taxes? Do you use the cotton gin to turn your cotton into a superior fabric for making better clothing for your whiskers, or do you save the raw bales for the taxman?

A field to grow cotton

There is, however, a way to use your precious manufactured goods to pay your taxes - the Smuggler. Every once in a while, a smuggler ship will turn up at your dock and offer to buy your manufactured goods in exchange for gold bars, which the cats will accept in payment. Obviously, the smuggler’s prices are not generous (it’s a business, after all), but in a pinch it’s a good way to turn all that excess furniture you have into something you can use to fulfil your obligations to the Claws.

If you’re short on a tax payment, you can still submit it, but the cats’ opinion of you will decrease along a 5-point scale from “happy” to “hostile”, a completely skipped tax payment sees their opinion decrease by 2, a partial payment gives a penalty of 1, while overpaying tax nets a +1 opinion boost (plus a reward), and overpaying tax dramatically gives a +2 opinion boost plus a more generous reward. The rewards for excess tax payments are either one or two selections from a list of various manufactured goods, with different value based on how much you overpaid your taxes. What happens if your opinion slips too far? The tax ships that visit will open fire on your colony, bombarding it with cannonballs for a while before leaving. These bombardments will destroy buildings and pathways, injure, and even kill your Whiskers, making it even harder for your Whiskers to rebuild and be ready for the next tax ship (which is still coming in two days time!). Later in the game, when you’ve got more significant resources, you can construct walls to protect your town from the cannons (since they’re simulated via line of sight from the ship, a bombardment can’t hit a building the ship can’t see), which is also useful against pirates.

Every few days, a ship loaded with supplies will rock up at your main dock and offer you the choice of several packets of resources, typically manufactured goods. These aren’t gifts, though; the cost of whichever packet you select gets added to your next tax bill. You can, of course, refuse to purchase any supply packets, but if you do, you get an immediate -1 opinion malus with the cats for your impertinence. Critically, the Supply Ship and tax-overpayment rewards are the only way to acquire the Machinery resource, required both to build and maintain all factories, but which can’t be produced domestically until the late/end-game.

The Whisker Ship will also visit your dock and offer a range of new colonists you can take on by spending Approval points, either by selecting individuals or accepting the entire shipment at once. As the game is now, Whiskers don’t seem to reproduce, so this is the only way to replace colonists that died of cold, hunger, or bombardment.

Bold (and adorable) sentinels stand ready to face the pirate menace.

Occasionally, a pirate ship will turn up at your dock and demand a ransom, typically in the form of high-quality produced goods like tailored clothes and machinery. Failure to pay results in immediate bombardment by cannon, in the same way as the Claws bombardment. Later in the game, the player can construct anti-pirate defences, like towers armed with cannons that automatically attack approaching pirate ships, along with various quests that include immunity from pirate raids as a reward.

Whiskerwood has an Approval system, whereby the experiences of each Whisker are tallied at the end of each day and assigned a score. Positive experiences like a good meal, warm surroundings, a nice dwelling place, etc. accrue positive points, while unpleasant experiences like homelessness, hunger, unburied bodies, cold, pollution, whether their neighbour snores, bland food, worn-out clothes, an encounter with a rude Whisker, etc. impose a malus on approval. Each of these things is weighed against the expectations of each Whisker (denoted by a star rating on their character card - Whiskers with 1 or half a star will endure pretty severe hardships, eating simple raw fish and living in a hovel without complaining, while a highly skilled or educated Whisker with 4 or 5 stars won’t tolerate anything but the highest standard of living possible, requiring a stone-built house with furniture, bedding, and accessible amenities like a bathhouse and dining hall) and the outcome decides how many approval points you have to spend the next day. Approval points can be spent on a few things, from recruiting new Whiskers, asking workers to perform a double shift, sending a ship to sea, etc. Balancing Approval is one of the trickiest aspects of Whiskerwood; you can’t bank it, you get a fresh amount every day, and the previous day’s approval is lost. Having a high approval but not spending it is pointless, while having low or zero approval can significantly curtail your ability to act. For example, it’s the depths of winter, your Whiskers are all cold and hungry, but you can’t dispatch your Deep Sea Fishing vessel to bring in a large quantity of fish, because launching the ship costs 20 approval and you’ve not got any!

Summary of Day #523's production, consumption, approval, and taxes

To produce the end-game resources your high-status Whiskers crave, you’ll often need to manage considerably more complicated supply chains - for example, to produce a high-quality meal, you’ll need to catch fish, grow wheat, grow peppers, and grow mushrooms; you’ll then need to process that wheat into flour in a windmill, then turn that flour into bread in a bakery. You’ll need to combine the fish with fuel and mushrooms at a smokery to turn it into a fish skewer; you’ll also need to grind peppers into spices and combine all three things- bread, skewer, and spices at a Fine Kitchen building, staffed by a Craftmaster and two Educated Whiskers. To improve this production, you can add table salt as a catalyst, which is produced by mining rock salt and passing it through a sifting tower (which requires piped water from a pumping station). That’s a pretty complicated process to make a meal, but it’s what your higher-status Whiskers will demand!

Monarchist Whiskers are a particular pain in the arse, complaining about the presence of factories being an affront to the generosity of the Claws. Even among the oppressed, there are always those who love the oppressor.

Since this is a colony sim, your main enemy is always going to be Winter. Even though the islands look pretty warm, when the dark season rolls around, temperatures plunge into the single digits and Whiskers will start to sicken and die if they aren’t kept warm. To that end, you need to build bonfires, heating stoves, and later Steam Radiators to warm the surrounding environment and make life possible in the depths of the snowy winter (and also to prevent farm ground from freezing and being unavailable all winter), but each of these methods both uses fuel and generates pollution. Later-game heating like the aforementioned Steam Radiators generate significantly less pollution (and since the steam travels from the boiler to the radiator through pipes, it’s possible to have the pollution-emitting aspect further away from where people actually live) but have an increased material cost to build; you need a lot of copper available to build the boilers and pipes to run the radiators, and to unlock the technology in the first place. So in the earlier game, your Whiskers will either be freezing in winter or complaining bitterly about the pollution produced by the bonfires keeping them alive, typical.

The slice view enables you to excavate huge caverns for farming mushrooms and digging up ores and stone

Each Whisker is automatically assigned to a particular guild from a list of four: Miners, Engineers, Farmers, and Explorers - being assigned to a job that matches their guild affiliation gives an associated productivity boost, and having all workers in a particular workplace have the same guild affiliation adds another boost. In addition, each Whisker can have advanced vocational or educational traits enabling them to take on more advanced jobs. An Apprentice is a worker with a basic level of additional vocational education. In a lot of factories, the first worker must be an Apprentice, and if none are available, the factory won’t function at all. To begin with, the only way to get an Apprentice is if one turns up to your colony on a Whisker Ship, but once you have Whiskers with advanced educational traits, you can employ them at a School and, through doing so, give additional Whiskers their education trait or guild affiliation.

Both workers on this cotton farm are in the Farmer's Guild, so they get a speed bonus.

Beware, though, if you’re thinking “I would just set up schools to educate all of my Whiskers to Apprentice level”, Whiskers with advanced education will have a higher expectation ranking and will be much more demanding when it comes to creature comforts! Beyond Apprentice, you can train Whiskers as Craftmasters, Educated, and as Sailors. Craftmasters are the most elite of the manual workers, and are often required to fill the last position in a factory and provide a significant boost to production by their presence. In some late–game factories like the Machinist, the only acceptable employees are Craftmasters, so keeping track of where your elite labourers are assigned is key to an efficient colony - having an Engineer's Guild Craftmaster working an unskilled job growing Flax while your Machinist goes unstaffed and there are unskilled Farmer’s Guild Whiskers hanging around unemployed is no good for the collective.

At least one Whisker with the Sailor trait is required to staff a ship - that doesn’t mean all the workers on a ship must be sailors (though there’s a production boost if they are).

Educated Whiskers are required to fulfil the need for bureaucrats, researchers, and producers of science-y things like chemicals and medicines.

This institution of classes even among the subaltern colonists is interesting; even effective slaves can live a somewhat bourgeois life, living in comfortable, warm housing replete with furniture and bedding, eating nice meals and engaging in activities like visiting a bathhouse. Lower-status Whiskers are not banned from enjoying these creature comforts, and will greatly appreciate them, but your educated and skilled workers will expect them and be deeply unhappy if you fail to provide (and they'll let you know via a big Approval penalty).

Later in the game, you can research and construct adorable railway systems to improve transit around your colony

Research in Whiskerwood takes the typical form of tech-trees unlocked by the spending of resources. You build a Research Lab, staff it with educated Whiskers, choose which technology/building you want them to work on, and they consume the necessary resources until the tech is unlocked. Each tech either enables the creation of a new building or unlocks an additional recipe for an existing factory (e.g, enabling the Ore Furnace to produce Bronze as well as Copper). You can build additional Research Labs, but Whiskerwood discourages speedrunning the tech tree by introducing a production malus on every research lab for every additional one you build (called Coordination). It’s still faster to have two (or more) Research Labs than one, but it is not 2x faster, more like 1.7x faster, decreasing with every additional lab built.

As of the time of writing, the endgame - which I presume involves boosting your military capability, declaring independence, and fighting the Claws to secure it is not yet entirely implemented, but will probably include more extensive defensive buildings and naval combat. At present, you can construct naval vessels and dispatch fleets to reduce Pirate islands, but at the moment the quests seem to be bugged, in that you can just repeat the pirate quests constantly and receive so many days of immunity that pirates cease to be an issue altogether. I expect that in the full release the naval aspect of the game will be considerably tweaked and expanded, but I certainly can’t say for sure.

Whiskerwood is a great game with enough complexity to scratch the citybuilder itch, and although it peters out a bit at the endgame as your industry becomes strong enough that your whiskers produce wealth and abundance far beyond the tax bill, this is pretty normal for Early Access games that aren’t technically “finished” yet. It’s not unreasonable to frontload development into ensuring that the early and midgame are more polished as a sort of “setting out the stall” exercise to intrigue interested buyers - a lot of early access games morph significantly during their development (Timberborn is vastly more polished now than it was when the Early Access was floated), and I certainly don’t begrudge the studio for this approach; I can’t wait to play full-fat 1.0 whenever it turns up.

If you love Timberborn, but wish it was a bit more like Anno, you’ll certainly love this, and if you like citybuilders in general, the Whiskerwood experience is well worth your time.

title: MTG Nauctis has whale gods, elemental krakens, and a new 'Black Lotus'
content:
Wizards of the Coast revealed details, art, and a couple of card spoilers for the first MTG set of 2027: Nauctis.

They teased their new evasive mechanic 'dive', brought back Descent, and told us about different creature types and their color identities. But more importantly, we got to learn about MTG Nauctis' gods.

While we only saw one at the show, Nauctis has a complete cycle of whale gods. It's only fitting that the largest creature on earth fulfils this role in the undersea plane. Salinae, the Ocean Mother gets cheaper based on your devotion to blue and makes 1/1 fish copies of every artifact or creature you cast.

While blue, green, and white whales appear in the set proper, the red and black ones are consigned to the commander decks. Taking their place in this mythic cycle are two sinister elemental krakens. One remains unspoiled, but Tecton, Malignant Horror may be my favorite visual design from the set, a huge tentacle monster made of whale skeletons. The effect is pretty straightforward actually: you draw a card when you sacrifice anything. Seems like it'd be good with blood or treasure tokens.

Here's what we learned about the creatures of Nauctis, and the archetypes they fill:

Seals are red and white aggro - the Nauctis equivalent of dwarves, they're skilled crafters.

There are two kinds of sharks: shark people are blue-red pirates while bestial shark creatures are red green. Goramou of the Coral-Taken is an example of the latter. She looks terrifying, but just wants to help you ramp.

Finally, we heard about the merfolk, who are in Bant in this set, found in blue, white, and green. They are central to the story, an ancient ruling culture affected by a schism around an independent city state.

Finally, we saw Nauctis' headliner card, which is Abyssal Lotus. It's a much less broken take on Black Lotus, which works just like the famous Power 9 piece, but firstly it only works if there are eight or more permanents in the graveyard, and it enters tapped (boo). Still, it's likely to be the expensive card of the set, especially the ultra-rare textless version.

Share your thoughts on the set at the Wargamer Discord.

title: [40k] Big Hat, Reviewed
content:
The hat, she is big. Specifically, I am posting from within the 1:1 scale Mark X helmet (in Dark Angels colors, necessarily) from Joy Toy. I paid my own money for it, and got the one with the stand and the included t-shirt.

The author, pictured. Credit: Greg Chiasson

As an aside, it is not lost on me that the only two articles I’ve written since my son was born have been about 1. sitting in a comfy chair and 2. wearing a dorky hat. I realize how this looks, but I don't generally buy things. I do, obviously, but only when forced. I cycle through two water bottles, and both have my company's logo on them. My main hoodie is also something I got for free. I haven't spent my own money on a computer since 2014, and only last year got a new phone, getting rid of an iPhone that was fully a decade old. So the fact that I've been instantly and furiously slamming the buy button on any Warhammer merch with a Dark Angel on it represents either intense personal growth or whatever the opposite of growth is.

Take a quick peek at this photo, and think about how your head would fit in there. Wrong, it’s bigger. Roomier. Cavernous. This helmet is enormous on a replacement-size human, but comically tiny on an Intercessor model, which really drives home how massive a Space Marine must be. This information may not rise to the level of useful, but it is at a minimum illustrative.

The big hat existed already, in an Ultramarines version. Many of us have purchased it, talked about it, and perhaps even reviewed it. If we did the latter, I haven’t read it, and you shouldn’t either. I will explain why: the Ultras version could not have been better than a 4 out of 5, because this is a 5 out of 5 and if painted as any other chapter it could - objectively - not be rated as highly. Equally, it could not have been worse than a 4 out of 5, because it is, at the end of the day, still a big goofy space helmet you can wear around your home, and categorically that cannot be a bad thing. So that review, if it exists, is not required reading; it either ends the way I already told you it does and your curiosity is now sated, or it doesn’t and is thus so wrongheaded in its conclusion that you can skip it.

I mentioned that the helmet comes with a stand and a Dark Angels shirt. The shirt absolutely whips; great design, is appropriately Dark Angelic, and better quality material than I’d expect, given the source.

The stand looks like nothing so much as an oversized piece of Warhammer terrain, which I mean as a compliment. The Dark Angels logo on the front is a separate piece, which makes sense if they wanted to use the same stand design for other, lesser, chapters.

It does feel like the Warhammer merch people are making up bullshit directly for me, and to them I would say: keep it up, I have poor impulse control. Lest you think that’s a joke, I want to point out that when the Dark Angels chapter banner went up for pre-order, there was a gap of less than two minutes between Rob sending me the link and me replying with a screenshot of my order confirmation. I know what I’m about here.

Much like that banner, I still don’t know where to put this gigantic thing. For now, it lives on top of my printer, and so every time I want to print anything I have to move it out of the way or it causes a paper jam. Admittedly that problem is specific to me, but otherwise: what is it like living with big hat? How practical of a wardrobe or lifestyle choice is it? In terms of the five main senses - I don’t have any proven psychic or psionic abilities, but I assume the helmet wouldn’t interfere with those, and it’s plastic so something like an electric Eel, or a direction-finding organ attuned to the earth’s magnetic field, should be fine - the results are surprisingly positive.

Sight: I watched some of Dune Part 2. The tinted eye lenses turn everything red, which is a problem generally speaking but notably makes the Giedi Prime gladiator sequence look insanely cool. This was all aided by the fact that it’s roomy enough in there that I could keep my glasses on the entire time. That said, the big hat does have a limited field of view, so if/when I go to an IMAX showing of Dune Part 3, I will probably not wear this.

Insanely cool to watch Dune through a Dark Angels hat.

Sound: Phoebe Bridgers’ Lost Weekend is a towering achievement, an absolutely titanic record. I don’t want to be reductive about this, because it’s a very good album that can’t be filed away or derided as sad music about boys - it’s weird and incisive and will probably rewire my brain the same way that Punisher did - but some portion of it is about her relationship with Bo Burnham, and a lot of the rest is about her relationship with her (dead? I should look that up) father. Now, as also the father of a daughter, if my kid grows up and writes an album this good, but where she talks about me like that, I would be very proud of her and also probably want to fake my own death to get away from it.

Anyway I can’t hear things very well through the helmet. The muffling effect is pronounced, and when music isn’t playing, it makes my tinnitus go hog wild.

Touch: You cannot be touched while wearing this, which is bad. However, that is what helmets are for, which is good. So this test fails, but fails by design, and so paradoxically it passes.

For the helmet’s part, where it touches the top of your head there’s an adjustable doodad that keeps it steady and comfortable. No complaints, really.

Taste: There is enough room to sneak a hand up in there and eat a small snack without taking the big hat off your head, but something like a pulled pork or even brisket sandwich would not fit. A popsicle or corn dog shape would probably work. Nothing bigger than that though.

Smell: There’s no nose hole up front, but the neck hole on the bottom is gigantic, so you can position your behelmed head above the Dark Angels scented candle and still get a whiff of whatever they were trying to do there.

I love the big hat, for some of the same reasons that I love the chair. No, this one isn’t nearly as useful, but it still amuses me that it exists, and I enjoy having it in my presence. I am going to go on claiming to be god’s only creation that is immune to propaganda, but I think we can look at the fact that I spent two hundred dollars on something to take up space I don’t have just because it was the right shade of green, and know on some level that I am lying. The trade-off for chaining myself to samsara a bit more tightly is that I can sit in my Dark Angels chair, wearing my Dark Angels shirt and helmet, looking at my Dark Angels art prints and painted models and (soon enough) anime wall-scroll banner, and feel incredibly, unspeakably, Normal. The feeling won’t last, but as long as they keep putting out new Dark Angels merch to distract me from reality I can skip from purchase to purchase like a stone across a pond and never have to confront anything. The stupider the better.

title: Pokémon Pocket lost 9 million users and 60% profit in the last year
content:
DeNA has reported its quarterly financial results, and it shows a continued pattern since early 2025 of fans gradually abandoning its hit TCG app Pokémon Pocket.

According to the results, which were published November 10, the revenue of the game business segment was down 28.8% year-on-year, while profits took a more significant tumble, down 60%. Now, in fairness, that's still $42 million profit, hardly something to cry about, but it does show that fans are continuing to bleed away from Pocket, despite all the app's new sets and changes.

In fact, a Q&A with shareholders revealed that monthly active users were down to 21 million in Q2, way less than the 30 million who were playing this time last year.

The company promised "additional initiatives and efforts" to help Pokémon Pocket recover its momentum, and pointed out that key metrics were starting to stabilize.

That's a reasonable point. The drop in players has definitely slowed down significantly in recent months. For instance, MAU dropped from 39 million in Q1 2025 to 30 million in Q2 2025. But between the first two quarters of this year it only fell by 2 million, from 23 million to 21.

We'll be interested to see what happens next, if the game continues to recover momentum this fall.

Let us know if you're still playing Pokémon Pocket? I got locked out last year when upgrading phones and never took the time to recover my account.
