We've got a separate article that explains the full history, and how it came to light. Here's the short version. In 1999 when WotC was getting ready to make the prerelease Clefable card, the initial version of the print sheet contained a small number of base set Raichus as well as the Clefables. The error was caught during production proofing and corrected, so only a tiny number of the Raichus were ever made, either eight or eleven according to different versions of the story.

All the copies of the card went home with Wizards of the Coast employees, who held onto them and occasionally teased fans by showing them off at public events. It wasn't until 2006 that they were confirmed to exist, and not until 2023 until any of the cards were graded. And so far as we know, a 2025 sale of one of the cards for $550,000 is the only time they've ever changed hands!

5. First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard

Price$700,000
Sale date 2026
Auction housePrivate
GraderTAG
RatingGEM MT 10

Ah, First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard. Ask a casual fan what the most sought-after Pokémon card is, and there's a good chance they'll answer: first edition shadowless Charizard. Perennially popular since its release in 1999, holographic Charizards have been a staple on the wish lists of collectors and fans for over 20 years, and a legend of playgrounds everywhere.

The first edition holo Charizard is particularly valued for its age, limited availability, and the recognizable image of one of Pokémon's much-loved mascots. Like all first edition Pokémon cards, this card is shadowless, printed without the dark border on the frame that was added later. There are a very few shadowless cards that aren't first edition, but it's the combination of the shadowless border and first edition logo that's the real certification of excellence.

In October 2020, a PSA 10 mint condition first-edition shadowless holographic Charizard was bought by ex-rapper Logic at auction for a sizeable $220,000 (£173,000), only to be surpassed a month later when another Charizard of the same specifications sold for $295,000 (£210,000).

A mint PSA 10 copy sold in 2022 for $420,000 (£334,000) via Fanatic Collect (formerly PWCC Marketplace) - but in April 2026, Collectr reported a private sale from Benjamin Be to Thiago Nigro for $700,000. That makes the First edition Charizard, once again, the most expensive playable Pokémon card in the world.

4. Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer

Price$1,769,000
Sale dateMay 18, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

It might feel odd for the third prize Trophy Pikachu card from the Pokémon TCG's earliest Japanese tournaments to sell for four times as much as the second prize card did in 2023. That's especially true, given both cards had the same perfect PSA 10 grading, both have a similar, vanishingly small population of PSA graded cards, and both were the only PSA 10 copy known to be in existence at the time of sale.

But that's exactly what happened: in May 2026, New Jersey auctioneers Goldin (yes, the ones from TV) sold the single confirmed Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer for a winning bid of $1.45 million - totalling 1,769,000 bucks after a 22% buyer premium. Why the huge price difference? Maybe the buyer liked the adorably tiny trophy; maybe the bronze sparkly finish simply looks a bit more like the gold of the No. 1 trophy card below.

Or maybe, in between 2023 and 2026, Pokémon cards have begun attracting so much more attention from the ultra-wealthy that the very rarest specimens are now a fashionable status symbol for billionaires (or those who wish to appear to be billionaires) to flaunt at each other.

Maybe the top end of this is mostly an ego playground for fabulously rich men who'll happily spend $1.77m - the cost of 4.1 million meals for starving people, according to the World Food Programme - on a 2.5 by 3.5 inch rectangle of cardboard, just because they can. Does it bring them as much joy as it brought a Japanese teenager at the end of one triumphant weekend in the late 90s? We can only imagine.

3. Trophy Pikachu No. 1 Trainer

Price$3,000,000
Sale dateSeptember 12, 2025
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingMINT 9

Sitting right at the top of the Trophy Pikachu Tree, fittingly, is 1998's Trophy Pikachu No.1 Trainer - extremely limited promos handed only to the winning Pokémon players at the TCG's second-ever sanctioned tournament, the 1997-98 Japanese Lizardon Mega Battle Pokémon competition.

Just like its promo prize siblings, the number-one Pikachu was illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita. This time, the world's most popular Pokémon is lifting a trophy in the air, grinning in triumph.

Supposedly, there are only 14 copies of this card, period. We've seen others sell for thousands upon thousands, but none have quite matched the price of the copy sold in September 2025. It's understandable - MINT 9 might be the best grading we've ever seen this promo get. No.1 Trainer Pikachu is a true winner, indeed.

2. Raincoat Pikachu - perhaps

Price$8,400,000
Sale dateSeptember 28, 2026
Auction houseFanatics Collect
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Raincoat Pikachu was created as a prize for a competition tied to the 3DS game Pokémon Art Academy in 2015; fans had to draw Pikachu in the game and upload it to the Miiverse social network. Six winners each got 100 copies of the promotional Pikachu card featuring their very own illustration.

This is a rare card to be sure, and in September 2026 a copy sold for a massive $8,400,000 (including buyer's premium) on Fanatics Collect - at least, it seems like it did. There's actually some doubt.

Reporters at Chase Society noticed that this auction listing was removed from Fanatics Collect entirely, which is usually a sign that the buyer has failed to pay. The listing then returned to the site. As of November 13 2026 it's still up, but scrutinizing the page source data shows that it has the "cancelled" status. There's an error in the data, it's just not clear where, so we're keeping an eye on this one.

1. Pikachu Illustrator

Price$16,492,000
Sale dateFebruary 16, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The new holy grail of the TCG, Pikachu Illustrator is a promo Pokémon card originally handed out to winners of a 1998 illustration competition run through Japanese magazine CoroCoro. Only 39 copies were ever created.

It's the only card to feature the 'Illustrator' title instead of 'Trainer'. The artwork was drawn by esteemed Pokémon illustrator Atsuko Nishida, creator of Pokémon's main mascot, Pikachu. There's even a unique pen icon in the bottom-right corner, seen on no other card.

It's unknown exactly how many Pikachu Illustrator cards are still in existence, but ten PSA certified copies have been graded as 'mint'. From January 2021 onwards, it was the most expensive Pokémon card to ever be sold at auction, with a PSA 9 Mint condition card selling for a whopping $233,000 (£167,600).

Though it lost the title briefly, in July 2021 Logan Paul (yeah, that guy) spent $4 million on the only existing PSA 10 version of the card, getting the purchase accredited by Guinness World Records as the most expensive Pokémon card ever sold. But the value of the card was actually even higher: to secure the trade, Paul also handed over a lesser PSA 9 version of the card, which he'd previously purchased for $1,275,000.

The saga of this card doesn't end there. In early 2026, Mr Paul went on to sell the card to one AJ Scaramucci, once again getting Guinness involved. That's because the sales figure this time was a frankly staggering $16,492,000.

We should add that Logan also parted ways with the diamond-encrusted necklace he'd been carrying the card around in (does a $1 card taped to a $2 million car cost $2,000,001?) But even so, it's more than fair to call this the most expensive Pokémon card of all time!

It's a pity it's so rare: Pikachu looks even cuter than usual holding an oversized fountain pen.

Bonus - Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack

Price$2,700
Sale dateUnverified
Auction houseeBay
RatingN/A

We're including a bonus curiosity because it's just too interesting not to mention. When Wizards of the Coast realized they had accidentally printed too many Base Set booster packs branded with the first-edition logo, they covered the errant symbol with a small black triangle. A simple attempt to avoid wasting resources has generated a much-prized collector's item, as fans now clamor for a rare Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack.

It's the packaging itself that's valuable here, not the cards inside, so don't go cracking one of these black triangle packs open if you happen to find one sitting in the back of a drawer (you lucky devil).

They're occasionally found in standard Base Set booster boxes - so if you have one you'll have to weigh up whether to gamble on the chance discovery of one of the black triangle booster packs, or whether it's best to leave the box unopened for its pristine value. Some of the black triangle boosters have fetched over $2,700 (£2,000) on eBay, depending upon their condition and which Pokémon is displayed on their cover.

Rare Pokémon cards FAQ

How we find the most expensive Pokémon cards

To compile this list, we come back each month to trawl the latest sales on global trading card and collectibles auction houses like Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC), Heritage Auctions, and Goldin Auctions. We aim to keep the rankings and prices as up to date as possible.

Remember that, like all collectibles and investments, the Pokémon card market is very volatile, and prices can change fast and often. If you're looking to buy and sell high value Pokémon cards, you need to take care to double check the latest prices, being very conscious of the website or auction house's commission rates and fees.

Which Pokémon cards are rarest?

The most valuable Pokémon cards normally command high prices because they're old and there are very few copies in circulation. Most originate from the earliest Pokémon sets, or are one-off tournament prize cards printed in very low numbers. First edition Pokémon cards, peculiar misprints, and desirable old promos all fetch very high prices.

How to tell if a Pokémon card is rare?

Wargamer has a dedicated guide to Pokémon card rarity covering the basic rarity levels of cards you can open in any pack. If you think an old card you've gotten hold of could be particularly valuable, our guides to first edition Pokémon cards and shadowless Pokémon cards will help you to identify them. It's also worth referring to our guide to fake Pokémon cards, as there are plenty of counterfeits on the market.

How to sell rare Pokémon cards

We have a dedicated guide on how to sell Pokémon cards, so we recommend you read that if you're considering trading - but here's the short version.

If you think you're holding a truly valuable Pokémon card, your first port of call is to get it protected by placing it in a thin, soft-plastic sleeve, then into a protective, hard-plastic 'toploader' case. Before spending any more money on the card, it's usually a good idea to show it to an expert in-person, to get their opinion on its condition and potential value. A specialist at your local games store may be able to help.

Then you should get it graded by a well-regarded, expert grading service - PSA Pokémon card grading is the most popular in the USA. Once you get the card back with an official grading from 1 to 10, and stored in a professional PSA protective case, you should have a good idea what price range you're likely to get for it.

Bear in mind that there's usually a huge difference in value between a PSA grade 7, 8, or 9 card (generally mint condition to the naked eye) and a perfect PSA 10 card (absolutely faultless, even when viewed under a microscope from every angle). The really high prices paid by top level collectors are only for PSA 10 cards, and a PSA 10 is very often worth more than twice as much as the exact same card at PSA grade 8 or 9.

If you don't find any ultra-valuable Pokémon cards in your collection, it's really not the end of the world. This is a game, remember - what you have got is a delightful collection to treasure and play with. If you want to share any new pack pulls or treasured classics with a community of fellow fans, you're most welcome in the Wargamer Discord!

To keep up to date with the latest news about new rare cards and any bargains we find, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: High Cathedra of Pride
content:
Welcome to another Trench Crusade Warband Focus. This week we're focusing on the self-styled first among all the Sins, Pride.

The Lore

Pride is the first of all Sins, and as such it's seat, the High Cathedra of Pride, is given privilege over the other six Serpent Heads in the incomprehensibly intricate machinations of the Court. The most recent holder of the seat is Eligos, the Grand Duke of Petals. They have not made any overt moves in the war against Creation recently, but they took the largest loan from Mammon in the history of the war in order to finance the construction of the automaton legions that took Rejika in 1872. From this beachhead into European mainland no doubt they will continue to press forward when the time is right.

Unwilling to let any who they march against be unaware of the glory of whom they face, all of the legions of Pride march under resplendent banners that glow with an eerie and unbearable light as a blinding perversion of the Heavenly Hosts they mock.

Defining Traits of the High Cathedra of Pride

Pride does not have particularly harsh restrictions, especially compared to some of the other Sins like Envy. As per usual, you must take either a Praetor or a Sorcerer to lead the warband. In addition you MUST purchase a troop flag, which either an ELITE or Desecrated Saint must carry.

Court Praetor Credit: Darius Minis

While your flag-carrying model is not Down or Out of Action, your entire warband scores critical hits on an 11+ instead of on a 12. This may not sound huge at first, but this will drastically increase the number of critical hits you can expect to land throughout a game. You'll see this the most with high attack bonus models like the Praetor.

It is against the nature of Pride to retreat from any confrontation. As such, if any of your models take a retreat move your opponent may place one Blessing Marker next to any model in their warband. Yoke Fiends within the Court of Pride are simply not allowed to voluntarily retreat without wearing a restraining muzzle.

Sorcerer
Credit: Darius Minis

Pride has very fitting SIN generation. If any of your ELITE models activate in Open terrain without touching any terrain that could give them the benefit of Cover they gain 2 SIN markers. Your Praetor and Sorcerer also have an additional method, if they activate within 18 inches and line of sight of a Wretched (friend or foe) they gain 1 SIN from their inherent sense of superiority. This generally means you will keep an entourage of a few Wretched near your leader, especially with the unique wretched equipment available to Pride. Pride lacks any unique method of SIN generation for its basic troops, but the peons can still gain SIN from the Desecrated Saint which gives one SIN to any model that activates within one inch of them (including themselves) and the classic Torture Instrument. But really, if you are playing Pride then your game plan is most likely all about the Elites. You'll usually start the game with a glut of SIN from safe out of sight activations when Cover isn't needed, but leaving your Elites in the open for SIN generation in later turns is more of a risk that you need to consider as the game goes on.

Battlekit Highlights

All of the Seats get their own special little toys to play with, and Pride has an assortment truly befitting the First Sin.

The Cloak of the Morningstar is a fantastic suit of armor. It is INNATE, so there is no risk of losing it in a campaign to a particularly unlucky Trauma Roll. Aside from being a way of giving one of your ELITE models a -3 INJURY MODIFIER without taking up one of their valuable hands, and as such I like putting it on a Praetor with the Serpent Assault Gun and the Malebranche Sword. It also makes the model completely immune to being made to take a forced move. For three Glory this item is an absolute steal. It can also be given to a Desecrated Saint, if you really want to prevent them from being moved around by tricky opponents.

Glorious Light is a defensive item available to your Hellknights and Desecrated Saint. For a mere Twenty Ducats you inflict -1 DICE to the Success Roll for all attacks that target the model with the Light. Added to a Desecrated Saint with a Polearm this can make them surprisingly difficult to shift.

Desecrated Saint
Credit: Darius Minis

Laurels of the Supreme is extremely dependent on your terrain set up. If you have a board with a lot of vertical play space it can be a fantastic boon. If you play on a more flat set up, it is a Combat Helmet that costs Three Glory. If at any point in the activation of a model with the Laurels it can draw line of sight to an enemy model that is at least 2 inches below it, you can give yourself one Blessing Marker. Up to 6 Blessing Markers a game can be a massive swing in your favor, and you don't need to begin or end your activation in the open to gain it, so a DASH action combined with a Praetors 8 inch FLIGHT movement means it is easier than it might first seem to get multiple uses out of it. It is less of an immediate Glory purchase than the Cloak of the Morningstar, but still a strong item.

The Lightbringer Rifle is an expensive weapon at 40 Ducats, and aside from CRITICAL it lacks any obvious enhanced killing power for its high cost. But it's special abilities are where it shines. Think of this as a reverse Laurels of the Supreme. Where that item revels in being above others, the Lightbringer is the raw venomous spite at any who dare to raise themselves above you given lethal form. You add +3 DICE to any Ranged Attack targeting a model that it as least 2 inches above the wielder. In addition to that, if the attack is a success the target will automatically Fall if it is within 2 inches of any open window, unattended door or ominous ledge. While not always lethal, this is always hilarious.

Eligos's namesake, the Petals of the Blood Roses are given to the most deserving of Wretched to scatter at the feet of their masters. A strange bit of defensive utility against BLAST weapons, the Petals of the Blood Roses let you scatter incoming attacks by 1d6 inches if they have the BLAST Keyword and would hit a friendly DEMONIC model within 3 inches of the petal-bearing Wretched. You must have line of sight from the initial target point to wherever it ends up. For just 5 Ducats this is a cheap utility item for the Wretched that you likely will have following your Praetor and Sorcerer around anyway as you will want to get the benefit of Superiority.

The Power of Pride

Light of Samael

Everyone's favorite SIN powered unholy laser remains our number one spell. You pick an enemy in line of sight and within 24 inches, and you roll Injury for them. If they survive, and are on 40mm or smaller base, you knock them back 1d6 inches. The utility of an attack that automatically hits at 24 inches is not to be underestimated, and now this Goetic Power specifically states that they move even if they are Down. As if we needed more ways to knock people out of windows.

Proud Defiance

Have you ever forgotten that Trench Crusade has a Morale system? Well keep on forgetting it with this power that makes you immune to the entire thing! Honestly not a huge fan of this power, but it can be of some use as Pride tends to be a fairly tall building Sin focused on a smaller number of more powerful models and only a few losses could potentially trigger a Morale check.

Too Proud to Fall

The other Pride Classic, I am less sold on this one however. While not going Down for 2 SIN per instance of it can be useful for your long term survival, especially if your model is in melee, the BLOOD MARKERS from any attacks that would cause the Down result still stack up. It can be a life saver for an attack or two, but don't expect it to keep you alive if you leave a model completely exposed.

Wounded Pride

Our newest ability, if a model without ELITE would place BLOOD MARKERS on the model with this spell, you place the same number of BLOOD MARKERS on the attacking model. Not exactly a rubber and glue scenario, but very it is deliciously spiteful and very tasty on a Hellknight.

Playing the Warband

Pride lists lean tall. Get your ELITE core going strong, with at least two of the Big Three included in every list. Those being Praetor, Sorcerer and Hunter of the Left Hand Path. I then recommend getting a Saint and a few Yokes and Wretched to fill in as needed. But taking a Hellknight for a banner bearer is also an option if you can't afford a Saint and don't want to give it to the Hunter. Remember, you are required to take a Troop Banner.

Hunter of the Left Hand Path Credit: Darius Minis

If you can do so safely, you want to deploy in a group around your Desecrated Saint to maximize SIN generation for your first turn, as you will want a lot of it and likely won't be able to freely get as much in future rounds. Your primary SIN generation relies on your ELITE models starting their activation's not in COVER. This is less safe as the game goes on, but is possible if there is large line of sight blocking terrain to take advantage of. Otherwise you may need to nurse your initial harvest of SIN for several turns.

The Big Three will live up to their name in a Pride list. You will likely not have any significant killing power other than them for a majority of lists so you really need to make each of their activations count. I enjoy really using the multi-kill potential of the Praetor when you can position them well. Taking one or two softer targets out with the Serpent Assault Gun and then charging into a different threat with a Malebranche backed up by the Light of Samael to add an extra hit that can push the target out of melee and generate another swing with that deliciously deadly Malebranche means you can significantly thin out the opposing force if you position them well.

Sample List

800 Ducats, 6 Glory

Elites

Praetor - 224D | 3G

Upgrades & Choices: Too Proud to Fall, Light of Samael

Battlekit: Serpent Assault Gun, Malebranche Sword, Sword/Axe, Cloak of the Morning Star

Sorcerer - 138D

Upgrades & Choices: Light of Samael, Proud Defiance, Blessing of the Serpent Moon

Battlekit: Trench Club, Standard Armor, Trench Shield.

Hunter of the Left-Hand Path - 140D | 1G

Hunter of the Left-Hand Path – 140D | 1G

Battlekit: Bow of Lethe, Head Taker, Cthonic Vessel, Standard Armor

Troops

Desecrated Saint - 161D

Battlekit: Polearm, Sword/Axe, Troop Flag

Yoke Fiend - 41D

Battlekit: Trench Club, Trench Club

Yoke Fiend - 41D

Battlekit: Trench Club, Trench Club

Wretched - 27D

Battlekit: Trench Knife, Trench Knife, Petals of the Blood Roses

Wretched - 27D

Battlekit: Trench Knife, Trench Knife, Petals of the Blood Roses

Final Thoughts

Pride does not exactly play differently than most other Court lists do. Your lists will usually act like more of a refinement of the classic Big Three lists, making each of them into the most powerful and dangerous versions of themselves. Your elites can be fantastically lethal and extremely difficult to kill if played correctly and that only gets more true in campaign games where you have access to the best Glory Items of the faction. Your heavy lifting will be done by your Elites, everyone else is there to sit bodies on objectives and support your star players by any means.

Embrace your clear and objective greatness. Let nothing stand before you. Aura Farm. And rest assured that if they impossible happens and you do lose a game, it's all a part of your master plan and you clearly meant for it to occur so you can set up your future victories. For the Duke of Petals.

title: "We took a huge risk": how luck, tenacity, and lockdown made the wargame Eldfall Chronicles
content:
Eldfall Chronicles feels like it appeared overnight, suddenly showing up in American hobby stores after distributors caught wind of a hot new skirmish wargame with gorgeous miniatures that had grown up quietly in Slovenia. I spoke to Žiga Gantar, co-creator of the Eldfall Chronicles universe, and CEO and creative director of publisher Freecompany, to discover how it came to be.

"I started working on Eldfall when I was studying in Japan", Gantar says, enrolled on a Masters degree in East Asian studies alongside his now-fiancée Tjaša Gaber. "I couldn't play many wargames because I was away from home, so I started working on my own".

Eldfall Chronicles' origins

Work started with the setting, the world of Calad. "History is in general my hobby," Gantar says, "in my home university I spent a lot of time studying European history", and while in Japan he "spent a lot of time studying culture, history, not just Japanese history, Chinese as well, Korean as well". This is the origin for Eldfall's setting, a fantasy world with distinctly East Asian influences where "everything is intermingling, cultures are cross-pollinating".

Gantar and Gaber hadn't long returned from Japan when COVID hit, and "university kind of wasn't a thing anymore". "Me and my fiancée decided If there's ever going to be a time to work on a game, it's now". "Tjaša predominantly went into graphic design, writing, things like that - she's been writing most of the lore for us". Gantar focused on world building and illustration. "It was quite a journey going from miniature painting and sketching on paper to full-on digital art".

Before COVID restrictions had fully lifted "we started putting our own money into getting the first minis made, opening a company, stuff like that"… "I started working with 3D sculptors to design things, art directing". He admits "we took a huge risk".

Eldfall's miniatures are beautifully designed, though the style isn't exactly to my taste; they give me the vibe of characters in a high budget Chinese MMO created in the Unreal engine, and I tell Gantar as much. "Definitely some of the influence comes from there", he says, "when I was younger MMOs were the thing. On top of that I'm a huge fan of games like The Witcher and the From SoftwareGames, everything from Dark Souls, Sekiro, Bloodborne, Elden Ring, those gritty aesthetics".

I can see his point. The Western-coded factions, like the Helian League, remind me of Eastern media representations of Western fantasy archetypes, from Berserk, to Dark Souls, to the Japanese book covers for the Game of Thrones series. The studio also aims to make its miniatures more realistically proportioned than other wargames. "A lot of wargames go one to four, maybe one to five head to body ratio - we often go with one to six, one to seven".

Unicool miniatures

While Eldfall miniatures aren't excessively busy with details, the details they do have are extremely finely rendered - they're more detailed than I can easily paint. That wouldn't be possible without a high quality casting process; it feels a bit miraculous that two first-time game developers with no experience of model production managed to find one. "It was a mixture of tenacity and luck", Gantar says. "We tried a number [of manufacturers], at least 12 that we exchanged materials with, checked what they can do, how helpful they are".

It was around the time of the first Eldfall Chronicles Kickstarter campaign in 2021 that the team was contacted by Unicool Plastic Manufacturing. "From the get-go, they were way more helpful as people than many other manufacturers". The firm's chief engineer "offered to test out a new material with us", and after some back and forth tests to develop the specifications, "we were the first game on the market using Unicool Hard Plastic, or Unicast as they now call it, for our whole range of models".

I've built Unicast miniatures from both Eldfall Chronicles and Corvus Belli's Warcrow; it's light, strong, is similar in hardness and flexibility to HIPS, and it captures fine detail like traditional cold pour resins. "It's only been evolving", Gantar enthuses, "before there were some problems with the material, like bent parts - especially with long thin weapons, and we really like to make realistic weapons - it pushed the Unicool guys to work on the material, and the latest version is really awesome".

Skirmish and dungeon crawl

Eldfall Chronicles has grown into quite an unusual product line. There are two main branches - the dungeon crawler board games, such as the existing Northern Winds set or the currently-crowdfunding Apocrypha, and then the skirmish wargame. The miniatures are cross compatible between the two lines, and while individual minis aren't cheap, starting to play the skirmish game is, because a playable party consists of just four figures.

"Obviously we want you to buy more miniatures," Gantar chuckles, "But at the same time, we wanted to bring the starting point low, so anyone can start playing the game". I've not played enough of Eldfall to give it a scored review, but my first impressions are very promising. There's a strong sense of characters having detailed and defined roles within the party, needing to coordinate their limited activations to achieve the mission. With every model so specialized it's very important to consider the capabilities of your opponent's force, as you can run into very hard counters for certain strategies that you'll have to think your way around.

"We play a lot of RPGs", Gantar says, "I spent a lot of time with things like Divinity, so I really like the whole idea of isometric exploration, and that's kind of the vibe I also wanted for Eldfall: I wanted people to make their own parties, outfit them however you like with upgrades and things like that". The model pool for list building is broad, since many models work in multiple factions and there are plenty of mercenaries, but so far the dedicated list for each individual faction is quite shallow.

More minis are coming: "in the future we are doing more reinforcement packs, more new factions, new faction starters". Fans are already keen to get play modes that will allow them to use more of their collection in a game, though Gantar doesn't want to do this just by lifting the points cap: "it would just bloat it up, you don't get any added value from it".

Variant playmodes are a big part of Eldfall; about a third of the range is made up of monsters which are controlled by AI and show up in cooperative or semi-co-operative missions. "PVE is huge for some communities, there's a lot of people who don't want to straight up compete", Gantar says, adding that Tjaša is one of them. "She likes to play things in an adventure sense, like together we're going after a monster". It's another aspect of the game that comes from Gantar and the wider team's love of RPGs.

Eldfall Chronicles Apocrypha

Freecompany's current focus is its second dungeon crawler board game, Apocrypha, currently seeking funds on Gamefound. There's no need to own Northern Winds to be able to use this one, and while it's set up for co-op with four players, it includes a true solo mode, allowing you to play through it with a single hero.

The core version of Apocrypha is a little slimmer than its big brother Northern Winds; to make it more cost friendly for board gamers it swaps out a lot of miniatures for cardboard standees. A pledge comes in at just under $100, with four hero minis and a hulking great boss. There are options to spend a lot more and get a lot more miniatures, of course, and every model has skirmish game rules as well.

Given the recent spate of controversies around delayed and incomplete crowdfunding campaigns, I ask Gantar how complete the project is and what remains to be done after crowdfunding closes. "The project is around 90 to 95 percent finished behind the scenes", he replies, "we are in the process of [doing layout] and editing for production, also finalizing miniatures, optimizing them, things like that". "We're just patching up holes, seeing where some lore can be added, or if we need to remove some lore somewhere because it tells too much", he adds.

Despite the bevy of cool miniatures coming in this release, Gantar says "for me personally, it's really interesting from the story point of view". "You have a monumental grand library in the Sand Kingdoms; beneath it there's a sealed away section, and things have started to stir there, knowledge that shouldn't have been written has started to appear in those sealed archives".

The entity known as the Librarian cannot enter the archives, so they've tasked a group of mortals to delve in for them and return with these apocrypha. "Our party of heroes have a hidden goal; a part of their party went missing 17 years back, in a previous prospecting expedition into the archives, and they are now back to see what happened".

In terms of new gameplay, Gantar thinks the team have done very good work with "a really cool taint and party progression mechanic". There are other parties in the archives who "can steal loot from you if you're too slow, if you take too much time doing side quests". That gives a sense of urgency to your delves. You'll also have to manage the growing taint that afflicts your party as they're exposed to profane mana. "Those were kind of difficult things [to design], but also surprising in a really good way how they turned out".

The Gamefound campaign for Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is open until November 24.

Meanwhile there's a growing chance you'll be able to acquire the existing range from your friendly local game store. When I spoke to Gantar he had just returned from the colossal SPIEL convention in Essen, Germany. "I was really busy with business-to-business meetings", he says, "most of the time I spent in my small cubicle office on the booth", talking to European, American, and even South Korean distributors. "SPIEL was quite a step up from last year", he reflects, "we've started being recognized by other players in the community - it's really nice".

There are a few Eldfall players in the Wargamer Discord community if you'd like to find some more knowledgeable nerds to talk about the game - and if you've painted any of the miniatures, please share them in our mini-painting channel!

Flowing FistsME7February 5, 2027

Pokemon sets FAQ

The list above tells you every set released in Pokémon TCG history - but there's more to the story of Pokémon cards than that! Read on for answers to some of the most common questions about sets, to help you get a handle on the hobby.

How many Pokémon sets are there?

As of January 2026, there have been 130 English language Pokémon sets that were legal to use in organized play at the time they were printed.

The pace of Pokémon sets picked up last year, with a huge bubble of fan hype and interest for releases around January 2025's Prismatic Evolutions, and shows no sign of abating. In fact, this year (2026) is the 30th anniversary of Pokémon TCG's original launch, so there's every chance the hype train could speed up over the coming months!

If you want to store a large collection of cards, our guide to Pokémon card sizes has their dimensions and weight so you can work out exactly how much space you'll need.

How many Pokémon sets are released every year?

Around three to four Regular Pokémon sets are released each year - usually accompanied by two to four special sets and smaller promotional packs.

For example, in 2025 there were seven sets in total, including:

  • Four regular sets - Journey Together, Destined Rivals, Mega Evolution, and Phantasmal Flames.
  • Three special sets - Prismatic Evolutions, White Flare and Black Bolt.

What are the different types of Pokémon sets?

There are three main types of Pokémon TCG sets:

  1. Regular sets: The TCG's mainline releases, Regular sets are the 'tentpole' events of each season, releasing at roughly regular intervals each year with a large number of cards. Regular sets are normally available in quite a few different product types, including booster boxes of 36 ten-card booster packs.
  2. Special sets: Also sometimes called 'Special Collections', these sets generally have a smaller overall card list and a specific theme that underpins their most prominent cards. Special sets don't get booster boxes and are normally sold in Elite Trainer Boxes (ETBs) and small promotional packs like Binder Collections.
  3. Mini-sets: A catch-all term for all smaller set releases that don't merit the 'Special Collection' label, but are still a distinct collection of new or reprinted cards. These usually come in their own seasonal or promotional packs, like the three-card Trick or Trade mini packs released around Halloween, or promo tins.

And - for now - that's it for our guide to Pokémon TCG sets! If you've got a favorite to support, or just want to join the hype about upcoming sets, come hop into the Pokémon TCG discussion in our Discord community! Chances are we're also salivating over the latest chase SIR, too.

Alternatively, we've got lots more Pokémon TCG guides to help you along - we can even help you answer the twin age-old questions - how many Pokémon are there, and how many Pokémon cards are there?

title: All 13 DnD damage types explained
content:
Thirteen different DnD damage types define the many ways you can slash, freeze, burn, zap, shatter, or otherwise dispatch your fiendish foes. Everyone has a favorite (No? Just me?), but hot takes aren't going to help you survive in battle. This guide is for anyone who wants to really understand the damage system in D&D. Knowledge is power, and it might just save your skin.

This guide covers key spells for each damage type, as well as monsters who are resistant or weak to each. Once you're armed with all that handy info, head to our DnD classes and DnD races guides for more tactical tips.

For now, let's get studious:

DnD Damage TypeExampleStrong againstWeak against
PiercingSpears, bitesRakshasa (if magical)Swarms, Ghosts, Treants
BludgeoningMaces, unarmed strikesSkeletonsSwarms, Ghosts, Treants
SlashingSwords, talonsNoneSwarms, Ghosts
ColdCone of Cold, Ice Devil's spearSalamandersLiches, Storm Giants, Fiends
FireBurning Hands, Salamander's tailIce Mephits, Scarecrows, TreantsSalamanders, Fiends, some Oozes
LightningStorm Giant's Lightning BoltNoneAir Elementals, Liches, some Fiends
ThunderShatter, ThunderwaveEarth ElementalsAir Elementals, some Undead
PoisonStings and bitesNoneAssassins, loads of Fiends, Elementals, and Undead
AcidAcid Arrow, Black Dragon's Breath WeaponNoneBlack Dragons, some Golem, Mimics
NecroticWight's Life Drain attackNoneMost Undead
RadiantAngel's weapon attackShadows, Shadow DemonsCelestials
ForceMagic MissileNoneNone!
PsychicPsionic Blast, Mind Flayer's powersFlumphsConstructs and Aberrations

Piercing

You duck the Giant's club, then loose a crossbow bolt into its ankle.

The first three DnD damage types are what you might call the Physical damage types. They're some of the most common forms of damage in the game, dished out by all common weapons. That means every class that regularly uses a weapon, from the Fighter to the DnD Rogue, will make use of these damage types.

Piercing damage specifically refers to stabbing, puncturing wounds, of the kind dealt by spears, bows, and rapiers. Like the other physical damage types, there are almost no creatures that are vulnerable to piercing damage, but also few that actively resist it. You'll mainly have trouble fighting swarms of little biting things, or ethereal creatures like Ghosts.

Interestingly, the tiger demon Rakshaha is vulnerable to piercing damage, but only when it's dealt by a magical weapon, and only if that weapon is wielded by a hero of a good alignment.

Piercing damage is also commonly dished out by monsters, from spear-wielding humanoids to beasts attacking with bites, horns, spikes, or thorns.

Bludgeoning

You deliver the unruly drunk a staggering knock-out blow, then whack him with a stool for good measure.

Bludgeoning damage refers to blunt force trauma, of the kind delivered by maces and warhammers, or a fist. It's the default for unarmed combat, so a DnD Monk will make immense use of this damage type, but again this is one type that no player will have trouble accessing.

Bludgeoning is arguably the strongest of the physical damage types. Similar monsters resist it, but unlike slashing or piercing, a few common monsters are vulnerable to getting bludgeoned, most notably Skeletons.

Slashing

You scream out as the Owlbear's claw catches your side, raking across your flesh.

Slashing damage is the third physical damage type, and it refers to cutting attacks of the kind delivered by a sword or an axe, or by a monster's claws. While few creatures have vulnerabilities, there are many that have resistances to multiple damage types, and then one damage type missing.

So for instance, Treants are not vulnerable to slashing damage, but they are resistant to bludgeoning and piercing. In a sense, they have a sort of pseudo-vulnerability to slashing by way of being resistant to other weapons. It certainly makes sense that a tree person would find an axe more concerning than a rapier.

Cold

A blast of freezing air jets forth from your fingertips, encasing the goblin in ice.

We've now departed from the most common DnD damage types and are now looking at damage that's most often dealt by magic.

Cold damage is a little less intuitive to imagine than fire, but it's still pretty straightforward. It refers to the pain and damage caused by sudden exposure to immensely cold temperatures. You'll probably need a spellcasting class or a magic item to make use of it.

In terms of spells, the DnD Wizard gets Cone of Cold, delivering a huge amount of AoE cold damage. Meanwhile, the DnD Warlock gets a fantastic defensive cold spell in Armor of Agathys, gaining temporary hit points and dealing cold damage to those who come too near. Monstrous sources of the damage type include Elementals, Yetis, and frosty White Dragon breath.

There are a few monsters that are weak to cold damage, most of which are some kind of fire monster like the Salamander. But on the flip side, a large number of monsters say the cold never bothered them (anyway). If a creature looks wintry and ice-clad it might be totally immune, while most fiends are resistant to cold damage.

Fire

Ushering patrons out of the burning inn, your arms are singed by a sudden conflagration.

Fire damage is self-explanatory: we all know what fire is and how it damages stuff. In terms of dishing it out, there are plenty of spells to draw from, and if you want to be throwing Fireballs nonstop, we suggest the Evocation Wizard could be right for you.

However, unlike cold or lightning, you can also harness fire using mundane equipment. If you're out of spell slots, oil flasks and a tinderbox may come in clutch to turn up the heat on a burnable monster.

Fire damage is a rather mixed bag. It has a higher number of vulnerable monsters than any other damage type (wooden or ice-based enemies beware) but more monsters resist fire than any other damage type, barring poison. In particular, if you're taking a trip to the Nine Hells, leave your fire scrolls at home. Fiends will have a field day with fire-reliant PCs.

Lightning

The foolish Bugbear jabs the artificer's machine with his knife, leading to a flash and the smell of singed hair.

Lightning damage refers to harm caused by high-voltage electricity, which you're unlikely to come across through normal means unless you stand on a tower in full plate mail during a storm. So it's to spells we turn once again, where the lightning spells range from small cantrips like Shocking Grasp to big hitters like Chain Lightning.

In terms of high-electricity monsters you're likely to meet, the Blue Dragon unleashes lightning on its foes, while Storm Giants can hurl Lightning Bolts from range. There aren't any monsters particularly vulnerable to lightning damage, but it's not a very resisted damage type either. Most monsters that resist lightning also resist other common types like fire and cold damage.

Thunder

The Shatter spell releases an eardrum-rupturing sound, cracking the crystal wall.

Not to be confused with the previous entry, Thunder damage refers to harm caused by an intense shockwave of sound. In fact, it was known as 'sonic damage' in fourth edition.

It's one of the stronger damage types in D&D, having only a few resistant or immune monsters, and being strong against Earth Elementals. It's also quite rare that you'll come up against it. If you want to avoid thunder damage, be careful not to piss off any Djinn.

Poison

As your stomach lurches, you glance at your goblet in horror.

Poison damage comes from contact with or ingestion of harmful substances. There aren't that many spells that inflict it, and in fact, this is a damage type that seems more likely to come from a monster, whether a serpent, Green Dragon, or countless other stinging or fanged monsters.

Unfortunately for those who do take the trouble to pick up a poison spell, poison is one of the least effective damage types, resisted by an enormous portion of the Monster Manual. Anything with a strong Constitution or no blood is likely to shrug off poison attacks.

Acid

'I'm mellltinng', shrieks the Lich, sinking slowly into the deadly pool.

Now we're getting to the good stuff. Unlike poison, which generally has to be ingested or injected to cause harm, Acid damage comes from corrosive, dissolving substances that are harmful to the touch.

It's a good DnD damage type because it's highly consistent. Though there are no monsters with acid vulnerability, very few monsters are immune to acid's (I was going to say charms, but that's not it) power. Acid does struggle against some inanimate creatures like the Mimic, but overall spells like Melf's Acid Arrow are reliable favorites. Along with fire, acid is also a damn near requisite for fighting Trolls.

Radiant

A beam of holy light reduces the Vampire to nothing but dust.

The next few damage types are the hardest to imagine, because they don't correspond with anything you'll encounter in the real world. Radiant damage, for instance, refers to the burning power of holy light. While some might expect it to be effective against all unholy, Undead monsters, it's only the darkness-dwelling shadows that actually fear the light.

While the special damage types we've seen so far are mainly the purview of the party's Wizard or DnD Sorcerer, radiant damage is more likely to be wielded by a Cleric or Paladin. You're unlikely to run into much that resists it, though if you're waging war on heaven, there are some strange celestial creatures that will only take half damage.

Necrotic

The wight's chilling touch causes your skin to wither.

The flipside of radiant damage, Necrotic damage is best described as 'unholy'. Rather than Devils though, it's specifically related to the Undead, who are both its main users and the monster type you don't want to target. Interestingly, while some Undead are resistant or immune to necrotic attacks, not all of them are. You're probably better off hitting a Skeleton or Zombie with Chill Touch than slashing it with your sword.

While it's often associated with evil, there's nothing that dictates that a practitioner of necromancy or user of necrotic damage has to be bad or good.

Force

Your bolt of pure magic impacts with the Hook Horror at speed.

Force damage is a somewhat indescribable category that's given to magical projectiles and weapons. Spiritual Weapon and Eldritch Blast are common examples.

Force is often described as the best DnD damage type, and while that honorific is largely going to depend on what you're fighting and how many dice you're rolling, there's no denying that it is effective. There are no creatures that are resistant to force damage, not one. At the same time, none are particularly vulnerable to it (even the Helmed Horror, who was vulnerable in 2014 5e). If a monster doesn't seem to be taking enough damage from your regular spells, it's time to use the force.

Psychic

The Mind Flayer locks eyes with you and your head erupts in agony, unseeable tendrils wriggling into your brain.

One of the creepiest ways to hurt stuff in DnD, Psychic damage refers to damaging effects that alter or harm your very mind. Inflicted by some of the spookiest monsters like the Banshee or Mind Flayer, psychic damage presumably feels like the mother of all migraines. If D&D had a sanity stat, this is the damage type that would deplete it.

Psychic is another very reliable damage type, with few monsters resisting spells like the DnD Bard's Vicious Mockery. There are some creatures, such as mindless beings like Constructs, that will be completely immune, however.

That's all the damage types there are. Now go forth and lay waste, and make sure you come join the free Wargamer Discord community to tell us which monsters you merked. Or, for more rules explainers, here's all you need to know about DnD languages and DnD level ups.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).
